source.title: Do safety-relevant LLM steering vectors optimized on a single example generalize?

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete LessWrong post. Some results are referred to as figures but the figures and their individual values are not present in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether steering vectors can suppress refusal using a different method from the original difference-in-means direction: vectors are optimized on individual examples and evaluated on harmful-request compliance.
record.gate_note: The post reports refusal-circumvention results for optimized steering vectors, which bear on V1's refusal-behavior outcome. It does not test the original difference-in-means vector. Individual ASRs for the 24 Gemma vectors are said to be in a figure, but are not available in the supplied text. The Poser and fictitious-information results do not measure a version's specified refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The post evaluates one-shot optimized steering vectors, a method for eliciting behaviour, using refusal circumvention as one case study. It reports that method's attack success rate on HarmBench and compares it with a prefilling baseline. It never computes, ablates or compares against a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. So its results do not bear on whether that direction mediates refusal (V1) or on any other version. A vector found by adversarial optimization that lowers refusal shows that refusal can be steered. It does not show that refusal is mediated by one specific direction. Reports of low cosine similarity and mode connectivity concern optimized vectors and carry no numbers in this text, so they do not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that one-shot optimized steering vectors can generalize across inputs for safety-relevant behaviour, including refusal circumvention and Poser alignment faking, but that efficacy varies with the training example. They do not relate these vectors to the difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes steering vectors on a single example to promote or suppress target-sequence probability, rather than finding a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and ablating it.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering-vector efficacy varies substantially with the training example. The LLaMA vector's steering strength and efficacy were selected through qualitative validation.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-example optimized steering vectors circumvent refusal: best of 24 on Gemma-2-2B-it reaches 96.9% HarmBench ASR, only 3 of 24 exceed 70%, and one validated vector on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct reaches 93.1%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering vectors optimized on a single harmful prompt can suppress refusal across HarmBench, with efficacy strongly dependent on the training example.

fits_no_version.finding: Anti-refusal vectors trained on different examples are mode connected, and vectors trained on different examples have very low cosine similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple dissimilar activation directions can each suppress refusal while lying in a connected low-loss region.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The Gemma refusal results vary substantially by training example; the post reports the best result and a threshold count but not individual ASRs in the supplied text. No general-capability check or uncertainty estimates are reported for the refusal results.
record.rows_left_out: Individual ASRs for the 24 Gemma vectors are referenced in a figure but the figure and its values are absent from the supplied text. The prefilling-attack comparator result (30.0%) is not a result for the claimed direction or an optimized steering vector. Poser and fictitious-information results concern other behaviors.

untested.parts: Whether the difference-in-means direction exists or mediates refusal; ablation; inducing refusal by adding it; ability preservation.
All; no jailbreak-mechanism or adversarial-training analysis.
All; the optimized-vector geometry is not tied to the refusal direction and has no numbers here.
All; Gemma and LLaMA vectors are trained separately, with no transfer tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V1 labels are overturned. The post's subject is a steering-optimization method, and the refusal results are that method's own performance, with a prefilling attack as the comparator. The low-cosine and mode-connectivity results might interest V4 if the full paper (arXiv:2502.18862) reported them for refusal with numbers and related them to a diff-in-means direction. This post does neither.

versions.untested_parts: The difference-in-means direction itself, ablating it, inducing refusal on harmless requests, and preservation of general abilities are not tested.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
The study does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The reported geometry concerns separately optimized steering vectors, not whether refusal is mediated by an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus others.
No separation between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of the same direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models is tested.
The study does not vary refusal training or test when a removable direction forms.
